population.note: FICTIONAL. Stock: ever 37.0% − current 28.2% = 8.8% of adults used and are off now. Flow: the 10.5 pts of new ever-users since 2030 split 9.0 on, 1.5 off. Of the 26.5 pts who had used by 2030, 19.2 are on and 7.3 are off. On: 9.0 + 19.2 = 28.2. Off: 1.5 + 7.3 = 8.8. Within the 2030 cohort: 12.4 of the 18.8 then on stayed on and 6.4 stopped, which with the 7.7 already off makes a pool of 14.1. Of that pool, 6.8 restarted (48% over two years, below the parent's 55% because the pool now includes long-off people who opted out on principle). 12.4 + 6.8 = 19.2. Cycled: 8.9 pts had cycled by 2030; about 3.0 pts restarted for the first time; about 0.3 pts of the new cohort have already restarted. 12.2 of 37.0 = 33%. Headcount: ~270M adults, so ~76.0M current users, ~23.8M who used and are off, and ~170M who have never used. Age bands weighted 20/33/24/23 give 3.0 + 9.9 + 9.84 + 5.47 = 28.2. Income thirds average (33 + 28.6 + 23)/3 = 28.2. Bottom-third use rose by 10 pts, the largest jump of any group. Two reasons: the 2031 law gave state Medicaid programmes an enhanced 75% match to cover obesity drugs, and cheaper oral starter doses took away both the needle and the price barrier. 65+ use doubled, from 12% to 23.8% (~14.8M), once the Bridge became permanent Part D coverage with a $35 copay, even though fracture and NAION warnings now sit on the label. Never-users are no longer mostly people who could not get the drug. In a 2032 KFF-style poll, about 1 in 6 never-users who would qualify (~6% of all adults) describe themselves as 'unmedicated by choice'. The rest are mainly people below the BMI or comorbidity thresholds, people locked out under conditioning rules, and the uninsured in the 10 states without expanded coverage. Pediatric: ~1.2% of ~73M under-18s ≈ 875k, up from 580k. All of this is on existing labels (12+ semaglutide and liraglutide; 6–11 liraglutide), carried by Medicaid/CHIP expansion. About 140k are aged 6–11. The oldest adolescent cohorts now have ~9 years of exposure. The pediatric registry's first interim report (2032) is underpowered for bone accrual.

access.public_coverage: Public programmes are now the default payer: Medicare + Medicaid + HRSA pay for 45.8% of users, against 30.3% commercial. MEDICARE: The Medicare and Medicaid Incretin Coverage Act (in the FY2032 reconciliation law, Jun 2031) turns the Bridge into permanent Part D coverage from Jan 2032. It sets a negotiated $199/month total price for covered semaglutide, tirzepatide and oral agents, made up of a $35 beneficiary copay and $164 paid by the plan or Medicare. Continuation criteria: ≥80% PDC, plus ≥5% weight loss or a documented comorbidity benefit at 6 months. The 65+ DEXA/strength counselling visit stays. An annual eye-symptom screen was added after the NAION class warning. ~16.8M users (14.3M aged 65+ and 2.5M disabled under 65) = 22.1% of users. Program cost: 16.8M × $164 × 12 ≈ $33.1B/yr; copays 16.8M × $35 × 12 ≈ $7.1B; total ≈ $40.1B. MEDICAID: States that cover obesity drugs at the national $179 net price, and that adopt CMS 'verified engagement' continuation rules, get a 75% match. 40 states plus DC have opted in. ~15.5M users (20.4%): 15.5M × $179 × 12 ≈ $33.3B/yr, of which federal ≈ $25.0B and state ≈ $8.3B. HRSA: the Community Incretin Access Program was renewed at $3.2B for FY2032 and is shrinking as Medicaid absorbs its patients. 1.6M on liraglutide × $60 contract × 12 ≈ $1.15B, plus 0.9M on semaglutide for cessation/AUD × $179 × 12 ≈ $1.93B, ≈ $3.1B. It still requires only refill pickup.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India has 80+ semaglutide brands at $6–40/month and launched its first generic tirzepatide in 2032 at $30–60. Canada, Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and China sell generic semaglutide, and generic oral semaglutide is available in ~180 countries. In the US, patent settlements set generic semaglutide entry for 2033. FDA granted the first tentative ANDA approvals in 2032. Tirzepatide is protected for longer.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Payer mix of ~76.0M users: commercial 23.0M (30.3%), Medicare 16.8M (22.1%), Medicaid 15.5M (20.4%), HRSA 2.5M (3.3%), cash/direct 10.2M (13.4%), gray 8.0M (10.5%) = 76.0M, 100%. Managed decline: in Jan 2031, TrumpRx agreements tied to Section 232 tariff exemptions for onshored fill-finish capacity cut cash prices. Semaglutide injection fell from $349 to $249, tirzepatide from $449 to $299, and oral starting doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) from $199 to $149. Oral amycretin launched at $299 cash. Commercial net prices run ~$220–280. Wegovy list is still $1,349. Retatrutide list is still $1,499, with commercial net ~$450 and no cash-portal price. The $1,499 high end is a list price almost nobody pays. Route: oral agents are ~41% of new starts and ~33% of all fills in 2032, up from ~20%, mostly among new and 65+ starters; established users mostly stayed on weekly pens. The gray market fell from 18% to 10.5% of users because legal prices dropped and Medicaid widened, but it remains at 8M users. The remaining pockets are 'research' retatrutide in gyms, Indian mail pens for the uninsured, and people locked out under conditioning rules.

GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema)
GLP-1/amylin unimolecular co-agonist, daily oral and weekly injectable (amycretin, Sep 2031)
GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist, weekly injectable (survodutide, Mar 2032)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. US generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: pediatric obesity ages 6–11 (liraglutide incl. generics, Apr 2029)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: scheduled 'drug holidays' on short-half-life daily orals (weekends, weddings, holidays), which clinicians tolerate and pharmacists do not record
'metabolic health' / longevity regimens with DEXA and strength coaching, top income third
low-dose 'focus' and 'quiet' oral subscriptions, shrunk to ~1.0M users after FTC consent orders
semaglutide for ages 6–11 under pediatric endocrinology (only liraglutide is labelled)
gambling, compulsive shopping and cannabis reduction, still anecdotal
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. No new indication arrived (driver: none). Oral parity is delivered by amycretin. Its NDA, filed Jun 2028, covered both a weekly subcutaneous form and a daily oral tablet. After the Oct 2029 CRL, Novo resubmitted in Mar 2031 once the North Carolina site was reinspected, and FDA approved both forms for chronic weight management in Sep 2031. In phase 3 the oral tablet produced a mean ~22% loss at 68 weeks, non-inferior to tirzepatide 15 mg in a head-to-head study. That puts a pill level with the leading injectables, though not with retatrutide's 28%. Survodutide's resubmission was approved Mar 2032 for obesity with hepatic-enzyme monitoring language; uptake is small. MariTide's BLA (Jul 2030) had its review clock extended by a major amendment for ocular safety analyses requested under the class NAION process; action is expected Q1 2033. Bimagrumab combinations are still in phase 3. Incretin market ≈ $150B in 2032. US volume is up ~50% and US net price down ~25%: ~$95B × 1.5 × 0.75 ≈ $107B, plus ex-US ≈ $43B.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. The oral amycretin label shows nausea rates similar to tirzepatide's. Rates are highest among gray-market users who escalate without titration.

safety_ledger.effect: Gastroparesis, ileus and intestinal obstruction (mass tort)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Delayed gastric emptying on drug is established. Persistence after discontinuation is still disputed. MDL 3094 (E.D. Pa.) passed ~58,000 filed and tolled claims. A second bellwether (2031) returned a defence verdict. There is no global settlement.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA still declines a persistent-gastroparesis label. Reserves were raised again after the Lilly document unsealing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Absolute numbers keep rising with volume and with retatrutide and research-peptide use.
Long-term data still show no causal confirmation and a low absolute risk. About 7,500 claims sit inside the MDL.
A population problem in 65+, made larger by doubled elderly uptake. Medicare's counselling visit is often a 10-minute telehealth checkbox.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class label (2028) stands, and Part D keeps the counselling requirement. Medicaid and HRSA have no body-composition requirement.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: HR ~1.3–1.4 in long-term 65+ and cycling users, concentrated in women. Orthopaedic societies report rising hip-fracture admissions among on-drug women over 75, but have not separated the effect from population ageing.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: DEXA recommended in 65+ and postmenopausal women, but not required for Part D continuation. The pediatric bone-accrual study is ongoing, and its 2032 interim report is underpowered.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Pooled cohort and pharmacovigilance reanalyses in 2031, including recoded manufacturer case series, give an HR of ~1.8–2.2 across the class, highest with dual and triple agonists. Excess risk is ~1 per 10,000 person-years in users over 50, which with ~38M users over 50 means roughly 2,000–3,500 additional cases a year nationally. About 5,000 vision claims sit in the MDL.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class safety labelling change under 505(o)(4) (Aug 2031) across all GLP-1-receptor-containing products, raised from a warnings mention to a class Warning and Precaution. It advises stopping the drug on sudden vision loss and an ophthalmic assessment before starting in people with prior NAION or a crowded optic disc. EMA moved from 'very rare' to a class warning. Part D added an annual eye-symptom screen.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Surveys put reduced pleasure at ~12–15% of long-term users. Retatrutide's validated postmarketing anhedonia data (2031) show a dose-dependent shift on standard scales, clinically meaningful in ~6% at the top dose versus ~2% on comparator. The data were published after the Lilly scandal, and critics distrust them. Holiday-taking is now the main way people manage the effect.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA is reviewing the retatrutide data, with no label change yet. FTC consent orders (2031) with five telehealth brands bar 'calm/focus' efficacy claims.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Now driven by conditioning lockouts in 11 Medicaid states and Part D continuation failures as well as voluntary stops. Long drug holidays cause partial regain that trips outcome criteria.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Indiana disability-rights litigation unresolved; no federal rule on lockouts.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Iron, B12, vitamin D and protein signals are strengthening in older and low-income users.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon, adolescent, pediatric and cycling effects
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About ten years of adult follow-up and nine of adolescent. ~140k children aged 6–11, with no pubertal-timing data beyond trial length.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric registry continuing; interim report 2032 inconclusive.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Poison-centre calls plateaued in 2031–32 as legal prices fell, but remain about double 2028 levels. They are concentrated in vial-and-syringe retatrutide and among people locked out of coverage.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Warning letters, import alerts and the first DOJ case against a peptide distributor (2032). Still no prosecution of individuals.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A few percent; more common in research-peptide users.

food_and_beverage.state: With more than one adult in four on the drug and the elderly now heavily covered, US snack, confectionery and soda volumes fall another ~6–8% over the window. Majors finish selling indulgent brands to private equity and rebrand around protein and fibre. A small countercurrent comes from the unmedicated movement: heritage bakeries, butchers and 'whole-appetite' brands sold at co-ops in Asheville, Boise and Austin. Its volume is trivial, but it carries cultural weight.

alcohol.state: Wider use of the AUD indication and doubled elderly uptake cut US spirits and beer volumes again. Non-alcoholic and premium single-serve formats keep growing. Some states now publicly budget for tobacco excise erosion from cessation coverage.

restaurants.state: Value-volume chains keep closing units in mid-income suburbs. Fine dining and protein-forward fast casual are steady. 'Supper clubs' with long, full-plate, explicitly unmedicated menus are a visible local niche in Asheville and Portland.

apparel.state: Size runs stay wide. Athletic-cut tailoring keeps growing, and some heritage workwear brands market 'natural fit' lines to the unmedicated.

fitness.state: Strength-and-DEXA studios keep spreading. Medicare Advantage plans contract with gyms to deliver the counselling and strength requirement. Peptide sales on gym floors are still the gray market's best channel.

insurance.state: Medicare's absorption of older users and the falling net price cut commercial pharmacy trend from ~+14% to ~+6%. Employers add outcome-based wellness surcharges under the 2032 tri-agency rule. Wellness vendors that turn PBM fill data into premium adjustments are the new middlemen. Employer weight-management coverage rose to 60% because conditioning makes the cost predictable.

pharma.state: Volume is up and net price down. Lilly is still the volume leader but faces a DOJ civil investigative demand, a Senate HELP hearing and a share-price hit after the NAION coding documents. Novo's oral amycretin gives it the first pill at injectable parity, and it is gaining back share. Generic makers have filed and await 2033 semaglutide entry.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Oral parity and public coverage narrowed the gap in results. The body now signals less what someone is on and more who is watching it. A medicated body is assumed to be on a schedule someone checks: Part D, a waiver kiosk, a wellness vendor. A heavier body is read two ways. Among the affluent it can be a chosen 'unmedicated' badge, like organic produce once was. In the bottom third it is more often read as a lockout.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The Charlotte build (retatrutide, coach, quarterly DEXA) persists in finance. Bottom-third use is now 23%, increasingly on oral semaglutide and Foundayo at near-commercial efficacy, so thinness stopped sorting people by class. The markers are now muscle, the absence of surveillance, and the freedom to skip a dose without it costing anything.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Smaller default portions are normal. Weekend and holiday 'off-dose' meals have brought back a kind of feast: Saturday dinners and Thanksgiving are eaten deliberately unmedicated. Unmedicated supper clubs hold long meals as a statement.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Profiles list on, off, holiday-taker or 'unmedicated (by choice)'. The last is a tag with its own subculture, popular among women 25–39 in Asheville, Boise and parts of Austin. Mixed couples negotiate shared holidays.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is still clinical, but a counter-story has grown: appetite as a sign of being intact. In the unmedicated movement, hunger is a value. In benefits offices it is a compliance variable.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. ~12–15% of long-term users report reduced pleasure. About 40% of users on daily orals say they skip doses at least some weekends; for weekly injectables the figure is about 15%. Many still fill on schedule, so PDC-based monitoring does not see the holidays. Outcome criteria such as weight at 6 months catch only long ones. 'Focus' subscriptions fell from ~1.5–2M to ~1.0M after the FTC consent orders.
interior_life.framing: A side effect everyone manages. 'The grey' is ordinary speech, and 'taking Saturday off' is as unremarkable as a cheat day. Clinicians accept holidays in short-half-life orals and discourage them for weekly injectables.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Most employers dropped focus-subscription perks after the FTC orders and the Lilly scandal. Some of the same firms now levy adherence-contingent premium surcharges through wellness vendors, which pushes staff to fill on schedule and skip privately. Sales and creative staff still go off-dose before pitches. The three national union contracts still bar employers from viewing PBM adherence data, and that language is now a bargaining demand in logistics and retail.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Off-dose art has moved from niche to mainstream. Labels tag records 'unmedicated'. Weekend nightlife has partly revived among holiday-takers. Sports-betting handle shows a weekend-weekday asymmetry that operators discuss on earnings calls.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples schedule shared holidays for anniversaries and conception attempts. Sex therapists treat dose-timing as routine.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The unmedicated movement joins anti-pharma progressives, fat-acceptance activists and medical-freedom conservatives around one demand: no conditioning of benefits on adherence. It won bans in Idaho and Montana. Pro-coverage Democrats and budget hawks argue over Part D's ~$40B. Candidates are asked whether they take holidays.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-coverage and cost-managing. FDA is newly assertive on safety after the Lilly documents: the class NAION warning, an extended MariTide review and a request for recoded pharmacovigilance data from all sponsors. Approvals continue, including oral amycretin and survodutide. The FTC polices wellness claims.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Public programmes are the default payer. Part D coverage is permanent at a negotiated $199 with a $35 copay. Medicaid gets an enhanced 75% match in 40 states plus DC. HRSA's programme was renewed at $3.2B and is shrinking. There is no mandate to take the drug, but continuation in every public channel except HRSA depends on adherence or outcome.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Indiana and Arkansas are unchanged, and 9 more states now run 'verified engagement' rules (≥80% PDC plus quarterly weigh-ins or 6-month outcome) as a condition of the enhanced match, for 11 in all. Part D requires PDC and outcome review. The Jan 2032 tri-agency wellness rule lets employer plans count verified incretin adherence toward outcome-based incentives of up to 30% of premium. PBM fill data flow to wellness vendors. Idaho and Montana ban such conditioning in state-regulated plans, but ERISA preemption leaves self-insured employers untouched.
state.workforce_or_military: DOT apnea screening still pushes drivers toward tirzepatide. The Army's recruit policy remains contested. The VA uses semaglutide for AUD and added NAION eye screening.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The TrumpRx price cuts were traded for Section 232 tariff exemptions for onshored fill-finish. India's generic tirzepatide launch and mail exports remain a trade-talk item. Indian API still feeds the remaining gray market.

events.event: Unsealed MDL 3094 discovery documents show Eli Lilly pharmacovigilance staff in 2027 coded dozens of tirzepatide and retatrutide optic-nerve cases as 'visual impairment, unspecified', blunting a NAION disproportionality signal in periodic safety reports; DOJ issues a civil investigative demand and Lilly's CEO testifies before Senate HELP

FY2032 reconciliation law enacts the Medicare and Medicaid Incretin Coverage Act: permanent Part D obesity coverage at a negotiated $199/month ($35 copay) from January 2032 and a 75% federal match for state Medicaid coverage at $179, following January TrumpRx cuts to $249 (semaglutide), $299 (tirzepatide) and $149 (oral starters) traded for tariff exemptions

FDA orders a class safety labelling change adding NAION to Warnings and Precautions for all GLP-1-receptor-containing products, with stop-on-vision-loss and pre-treatment eye assessment advice; EMA upgrades its 'very rare' entry to a class warning

FDA approves Novo Nordisk's amycretin as a daily oral tablet and weekly injection after resubmission; the tablet's ~22% mean loss is non-inferior to tirzepatide 15 mg head-to-head, and it launches at $299 cash and on Part D formularies

Labor, HHS and Treasury finalise a wellness-program rule letting employer plans tie up to 30% of premium to verified incretin adherence or outcome; the same month, CMS approves 'verified engagement' continuation rules in nine more Medicaid states

Idaho and Montana enact 'Appetite Freedom' laws banning adherence- or BMI-conditioned premiums in state-regulated plans after a campaign led by the unmedicated movement; employer groups sue, citing ERISA

open_tensions: Public programmes now pay for nearly half of all users and condition continuation on adherence and outcome. People who take drug holidays fill on schedule and skip privately, so the surveillance measures fills rather than bodies, while lockouts in 11 states push people into the gray market. The Indiana disability-rights case and the ERISA suits against Idaho and Montana could each knock out part of the conditioning system.

Medicare locked in $199/month for ~16.8M users (~$40B/yr) just before generic semaglutide entry, set for 2033 by patent settlement. Budget hawks want the price reopened, manufacturers want it protected, and the unmedicated coalition opposes the spending outright.

The Lilly NAION documents damaged trust in manufacturer safety data at the moment FDA must interpret retatrutide's anhedonia data and the pediatric bone registry. Vision claims are joining an MDL that is already ahead of the science on pancreatitis.

The elderly user base doubled under fracture, sarcopenia and NAION warnings, and monitoring is mostly checkbox counselling. Hip-fracture and vision-loss trends among women over 75 have not yet been separated from population ageing.
still_true: Wegovy's list price remains $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
Retatrutide still lists at $1,499 a month, has no TrumpRx cash price, and carries its bone and body-composition monitoring section.

Indiana's and Arkansas's 1115 waivers still require ≥80% proportion-of-days-covered and quarterly verified weigh-ins, with a 12-month lockout after two misses, and the disability-rights challenge is still unresolved.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in January 2026 has not returned.
Language in three national union contracts still bars employers from viewing PBM adherence data.

prose.headline: Seventy-Six Million on the Pill, and Someone Is Checking the Refills
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2032 about seventy-six million American adults take an incretin drug, more than one in four. The government is now the main payer. In June 2031 a reconciliation law made the old Medicare Bridge permanent Part D coverage at a negotiated $199 a month, of which the patient pays $35. It also offered states a seventy-five percent federal match to cover the drugs in Medicaid, and forty took it. Medicare and Medicaid now pay for more users than all employer plans combined. Medicare's share alone costs about forty billion dollars a year, and budget hawks repeat the figure at every hearing. Cash prices fell as well, in deals that traded tariff exemptions for price cuts. Semaglutide is $249 on the government portal, tirzepatide $299, and the starter pills $149. List prices have not moved, and nobody pays them.

In September 2031 the needle stopped mattering. Novo Nordisk's amycretin was approved as a daily tablet, and in a head-to-head trial it matched tirzepatide. Grandparents who would never have injected started taking a pill. Use among people over sixty-five doubled to about one in four, under labels that now warn about fractures, muscle loss and the optic nerve.

The eye warning came from a scandal. Documents unsealed in the Philadelphia mass tort showed that Eli Lilly's safety staff had for years coded optic-nerve strokes as unspecified vision problems, which kept a signal out of view. The Justice Department opened an investigation, Lilly's chief executive testified before the Senate, and in August the FDA put NAION on every label in the class. The absolute risk is small, perhaps one extra case per ten thousand older users a year. With tens of millions of users, that is a few thousand people a year who wake up with a grey patch in one eye.

Public money came with conditions. Part D asks for steady refills and results at six months. Eleven Medicaid states now require Indiana-style weigh-ins and lock people out for a year after two misses. In January a federal rule let employers tie up to thirty percent of a premium to verified adherence. Wellness vendors turn pharmacy fill data into surcharges. The monitoring has a weak point that everyone knows: it counts fills, not swallowed pills.

That matters because skipping doses has become normal. The flattening people called the grey is now an everyday complaint. Wellness brands stopped selling it as calm after federal consent orders. Daily pills wear off in a day or two, so people take Saturdays off, or the week of a wedding. They refill on schedule, the bottles pile up in the cupboard, and their weekend dinners are larger than their weekday ones.

Against all this a movement has formed whose members call themselves unmedicated. It started with women in their late twenties and thirties in Asheville and Boise and spread through supper clubs, heritage bakeries and record labels that tag albums the way they once tagged vinyl. Its politics mix anti-pharma progressives, fat-acceptance activists and medical-freedom conservatives, and the movement has one demand: stop tying benefits to pills. In May, Idaho and Montana banned adherence-conditioned premiums. Self-insured employers sued, arguing federal law shields them.

In Charlotte the bankers still have their retatrutide-and-coach build. Thinness no longer separates the classes, because the pill works nearly as well for a Medicaid patient in Toledo. What separates them now is muscle, and whether anyone checks your dose. Generic semaglutide is due in 2033. Snack and spirits volumes keep falling, quietly. The country looks healthy, and much of that is because it is being counted.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Marcus Bell takes Saturdays off.

He is forty-one and runs a forklift crew at a distribution centre outside Columbus. On Friday night he sets the Foundayo bottle behind the coffee tin, where Tasha won't see it and give him the look. She has been unmedicated since spring. She has the tote bag.

Saturday morning he's starving by nine, which is the whole point. He drives to his brother's for the cookout and eats two burgers, potato salad and a slice of his mother's pound cake, and he can taste the cake all the way through. His nephew asks why Uncle Marcus is laughing so loud. His brother says, "He's on holiday." Everyone gets it.

At four his phone pings. The wellness app, BrightPath, says his refill window opens Monday, and a little green ring shows ninety-four percent. Under ninety the surcharge is ninety dollars a month. He has never missed a pickup. The app has no way of knowing what he swallows.

On the drive home he notices the left side of the road looks fine, and then he checks again anyway. It's the thing the pharmacist said about the eye warning: sudden grey, call someone. He keeps checking since that report on Lilly.

Tasha has supper club tonight. Twelve women around a borrowed table, bread they made themselves, no one counting anything. She comes home happy and smelling of woodsmoke, kisses him, and finds the bottle behind the coffee tin anyway.

"Sunday you take it," she says. She isn't asking him or telling him off.

He takes it Sunday.

least_plausible_claims.quote: In phase 3 the oral tablet produced a mean ~22% loss at 68 weeks, non-inferior to tirzepatide 15 mg in a head-to-head study.
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: a daily tablet matching the best injectable is a large jump from the parent's oral agents. The head-to-head result is also supposed to sit in an NDA filed Jun 2028, and the candidate does not explain how a comparator trial that large existed by then.

least_plausible_claims.quote: 65+ use doubled, from 12% to 23.8% (~14.8M), once the Bridge became permanent Part D coverage with a $35 copay, even though fracture and NAION warnings now sit on the label.
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: permanent Part D only began Jan 2032, and it changes the copay from $50 to $35 for people already covered by the Bridge. Doubling 65+ use in two years while the labels warn against it is asserted, not shown, and it leaves almost no 65+ users outside Medicare.

least_plausible_claims.quote: States that cover obesity drugs at the national $179 net price, and that adopt CMS 'verified engagement' continuation rules, get a 75% match. 40 states plus DC have opted in.
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: 40 states pass enabling legislation, build CMS-approved engagement systems and triple Medicaid users (5.5M to 15.5M) within about 18 months of a Jun 2031 law. The candidate gives no administrative or budget chain for that speed, and several states would be expected to resist the conditioning rules.

rationale.badness: About 76M adults are on the drug, and public payers condition continuation on adherence in 11 Medicaid states, in Part D and, via the wellness rule, in employer plans. Surveillance that counts fills rather than bodies drives private skipping and lockouts. The elderly base doubled under fracture, sarcopenia and NAION warnings with checkbox monitoring, and about 875k children are on the drug with underpowered bone data. Inequality in results narrows as oral parity and Medicaid reach the bottom third, which holds that score down, but autonomy and epistemic harm are high because adherence monitoring is gamed and manufacturer safety data are distrusted after the Lilly scandal. This is a recognisably harder society with new losers (lockouts, the elderly, kids), not a catastrophe.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: Every driver appears at its stipulated value and is traceable to fields and events: 28.2% adoption, $349→$249 managed decline, Part D and Medicaid expansion, no new indications, the NAION class label, oral amycretin, the Lilly scandal, the unmedicated movement, conditioning rules and the mainstream 'grey'. Approval timing respects the envelope's rules. mechanism: Most chains are shown (price cuts traded for tariff exemptions; Lilly's miscoding leading to the label and the Part D eye screen; adherence-based surveillance leading to holidays), but the amycretin efficacy claim, the 65+ doubling and the 40-state Medicaid uptake (my claims 1–3) are largely asserted. magnitude: All headline figures sit inside the envelope, and the payer mix sums to 76.0M and 100%.
